svg.aria-label: Diagram: Microsoft Entra lifecycle workflows structure, triggers, scheduling and limits. A workflow has three parts: general information, tasks, and execution conditions, where an execution condition combines a scope defining who is affected and a trigger defining when the workflow runs. The four supported scheduled triggers are attribute changes, group membership change, time based attribute, and sign-in inactivity. Time based triggers fire relative to a date attribute such as employeeHireDate, with an offsetInDays range of 180 days, or minus 180 to plus 180 via the API where negative means before the attribute date and positive means after. Newly created workflows are enabled by default but scheduling must be enabled manually, and once enabled the workflow is evaluated on an interval set in workflow settings with a default of three hours, configurable from 1 to 24 hours. If a user account or workflow is configured after the intended processing time, lifecycle workflows still attempt to process the user provided setup completes within three days of the original processing time, but this catch-up does not apply to the Time based attribute V2 preview trigger. Running a workflow on demand does not evaluate execution conditions at all and applies the tasks regardless, and on-demand selection is limited to 10 users, making it a testing tool rather than a bulk remediation tool. Service limits are 100 workflows per tenant, 25 tasks per workflow, 100 custom task extensions per tenant, 5 administrative scopes per workflow, and a custom task extension timeout between 30 minutes and 3 hours. Lifecycle workflows differ from dynamic groups by managing static groups with no dynamic group rule needed, needing no rule per group because the rule scopes users rather than groups, supporting attributes dynamic groups cannot such as a number of days before a hire date, and being able to act on the group itself rather than only its membership. Workflows can disable and remove user accounts, assign and remove access packages, and extend into Logic Apps. Versioning creates separate workflows reported differently in logs, and history can be viewed by users, runs or tasks. Licensing requires Microsoft Entra ID Governance or Microsoft Entra Suite, and the delegated role is Lifecycle Workflows Administrator.
svg.title: A small well-shaped engine bolted to a field in your HR system
svg.text: The trigger is a date attribute on a user object. Everything else rests on that field being right.
A workflow is tasks + an execution condition, and the condition is two questions: who (scope) and when (trigger).
Four triggers, each answering “when did a fact become true?”
TRIGGER
FIRES WHEN
NATURAL USE
Time based attribute
a date attribute reaches an offset
joiner and leaver
Attribute changes
“the attribute you defined is changed”
mover — department, title
Group membership change
a user is added to or removed from a group
access-driven events
Sign-in inactivity
“a user has not signed in over a specific
time period”
the leaver nobody reported
Sign-in inactivity is the only trigger that needs nobody to tell the truth — the platform observes it. Keep it on regardless.
The time offset is signed via the API: “-180 - 180 days… negative… before the timeBasedAttribute… positive… afterwards”.
So −7 is “a week before they start” and +30 is “a month after they left”: both ends of employment in one integer.
Three details that are not where you’d look
1. Enabled is not scheduled. “Newly created workflows are
enabled by default, scheduling… must be enabled manually.”
A correct, reviewed workflow can simply never run.
2. Late data has a three-day grace, then the run is gone.
And no grace at all on Time based attribute V2 (Preview).
3. Run on demand ignores the scope you wrote: it applies
the tasks “regardless of whether the execution conditions
are met”. Capped at 10 users — a test tool, not a backfill.
Service limits, and what they imply
Workflows per tenant
Tasks per workflow
Custom task extensions per tenant
Administrative scopes per workflow
Extension timeout range
30 min – 3 hr
100 is the one that shapes design: do not build one per
department. Rules scope USERS, not groups. Limits are soft.
Cadence is the real precision limit
Evaluated on an interval set in workflow settings — “default of three hours”, configurable only within 1–24 hours.
So a leaver task is never instant. If the requirement is “access gone at the moment of termination”, this is the wrong tool.
Lifecycle workflows versus dynamic groups
Manages static groups
“you don’t need a dynamic group rule” — membership stays explicit and auditable
No rule per group
rules “determine the scope of users… not which group”
Reaches attributes groups cannot
“a certain number of days before the employeeHireDate attribute value”
Acts on the group itself
“not just the membership”
The split: dynamic groups answer “who is currently X”. Lifecycle workflows answer “what happens N days either side of X
becoming true”. Membership is a state; a lifecycle event is a moment, and only one of these tools has a clock.
The number to watch is not failures
The overview reports total processed users, processed users with failures, failed tasks, number of tasks and current version.
A leaver workflow with zero failures and four processed users in a month when eleven people left is not healthy. Failures mean
the tasks broke; a low processed count means the trigger matched nobody — which is what this feature is actually prone to.
Downstream of HR by design: “HR provisioning manages the creation and attribute updates of user accounts” while workflows
“provide additional automation of tasks”. So fix the feed first. Licence: ID Governance or Entra Suite, as for post #56.
Sources: What are lifecycle workflows?, Understanding lifecycle workflows, and Microsoft Entra ID Governance service limits, on Microsoft Learn.
